messages.subject: Re: Trapping webs: multipliers and right-truncation
parts:
Bill/List:

Trapping webs do present some inherent difficulties. Truncation does
offer some help, but recognize that truncation is a reduction of data,
and any reduction in data will result in concomitant reduction in precision.

For particularly vagile species, Clethrionomys in my experience, and I
would not be surprised if Peromyscus are similar; many animals encounter
traps in the outer rings because the area sampled by the outer rings of
a web is large relative to inner rings. Hence truncation of the outer
rings is common. See Section 6.8.5 of Buckland et al. (2001:221) for an
example dealing with Peromyscus, where right truncation was employed.

The use of left-truncation for point transect data (of which trapping
webs are a special case) is not recommended, as it is critical that you
produce estimates of h(0) which is the derivative of the detection
function at the centre of the web; you need all the information you can
get near the centre of the web, tossing some of it is a poor idea.

Finally with regard to adjusting for g(0)<1. Having new individuals
entering your sample near the end of a trapping session is not
necessarily an indication of g(0)<1, an alternative explanation is that
your population is not closed for 4 days, and hence D-hat is changing
during your study. Recognize that estimating g(0) requires not only a
point estimate, but also an estimate of the precision with which you
have estimated g(0). So you cannot rely on an ad hoc method of
estimating g(0), but rather would need a method capable of producing a
measure of precision as well.

In summary consult the worked example in Buckland et al. (2001) that
references data from Anderson et al. (1983) on the same species as your
study organism.

Bill Kronland wrote:

> >I have a pair of concerns regarding trapping webs and was hoping someone out there could shed some light on the subject. I ran a number of webs in a burned ponderosa pine forest on salvage logged and non-logged treatments. Peromyscus species comprised the bulk of the captures.
> >
> >1) Captures consistantly increased with distance from the web's center. As a result, the detection functions fit to the data produce denstiy estimates lower than what was observed. Right-truncation works to a degree, but not without producing very large confidence intervals and greater CV values. Left-truncation drives the estimate down further.
> > Is this a common problem with trapping webs and how is it dealt with?
> >
> >2) Mark-recapture data showed that the g(0)=1 assumption was met with varying success. That is, I oftern had new individuals appearing on the last day of trapping (4 trap nights). The users guide for program DISTANCE suggests dividing the density estimate by the observed g(0) in these cases. I have ideas on how to calculate a value for g(0), but wanted to hear how other people have approached this issue first.
